malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Changing only the distribution name to mimic a popular package is a classic supply chain attack vector. This enables attackers to trick users or automated systems into installing a package that appears legitimate but is controlled by the attacker, opening the door for future malicious updates or payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior is for the distribution name and import name to match, and for package metadata to be unique and not copied verbatim from another package. Here, the distribution name is changed to hijack the trust and popularity of the original package, while all other metadata and code remain identical.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate forks may rename a package for new features or maintenance, but typically both the distribution and import names are changed, and the intent is clearly documented. Copying only the distribution name without any code or documentation changes is not standard practice.

setup.py and metadata fields (description, links, classifiers) are copied verbatim from a popular package

Presence of a package directory named 'certifi' inside a distribution named 'certify'

This is designed to deceive users and automated systems into installing it instead of the real package, enabling supply chain attacks such as dependency confusion and StarJacking. Even if no malicious code is present yet, this tactic allows attackers to later introduce malicious payloads or hijack trust in the ecosystem.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated using base64 encoding, automatically writes and executes a new Python script at import-time, and initiates network communication with an external, attacker-controlled server to fetch and execute additional code. detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Python packages that contain base64-encoded payloads in __init__.py or other early-loading files, especially those that decode and execute code at import-time. Watch for creation and execution of temporary Python scripts with randomized names in the current working directory. Flag network requests from Python processes to suspicious or non-standard URLs, particularly those masquerading as image files but serving plaintext or executable code. Correlate with package metadata (recently published, low download counts, names similar to popular packages) for additional context and risk scoring.
